input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

[RID:web:paper:133adeedffc6] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2109.05633v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.05633v1" title="Generating Datasets of 3D Garments with Sewing Patterns"
Garments are ubiquitous in both real and many of the virtual worlds. They are highly deformable objects, exhibit an immense variety of designs and shapes, and yet, most garments are created from a set of regularly shaped flat pieces. Exploration of garment structure presents a peculiar case for an object structure estimation task and might prove useful for downstream tasks of neural 3D garment modeling and reconstruction by providing strong prior on garment shapes. To facilitate research in these directions, we propose a method for generating large synthetic datasets of 3D garment designs and their sewing patterns. Our method consists of a flexible description structure for specifying parametric sewing pattern templates and the automatic generation pipeline to produce garment 3D models with little-to-none manual intervention. To add realism, the pipeline additionally creates corrupted versions of the final meshes that imitate artifacts of 3D scanning.
  With this pipeline, we created the first large-scale synthetic dataset of 3D garment models with their sewing patterns. The dataset contains more than 20000 garment design variations produced from 19 different base types. Seven of these garment types are specifically designed to target evaluation of the generalization across garment sewing pattern topologies.

[RID:web:paper:b3951564c2f1] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2108.06959v2" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.06959v2" title="WikiChurches: A Fine-Grained Dataset of Architectural Styles with Real-World Challenges"
We introduce a novel dataset for architectural style classification, consisting of 9,485 images of church buildings. Both images and style labels were sourced from Wikipedia. The dataset can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, as it combines numerous real-world challenges: fine-grained distinctions between classes based on subtle visual features, a comparatively small sample size, a highly imbalanced class distribution, a high variance of viewpoints, and a hierarchical organization of labels, where only some images are labeled at the most precise level. In addition, we provide 631 bounding box annotations of characteristic visual features for 139 churches from four major categories. These annotations can, for example, be useful for research on fine-grained classification, where additional expert knowledge about distinctive object parts is often available. Images and annotations are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5166987

[RID:web:paper:8425ac5de940] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="2006" score=1.00 cite_key="web_ballinger_2006_experimental_study_of_energy_minimizing_point_co" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611451v3" title="Experimental study of energy-minimizing point configurations on spheres"
In this paper we report on massive computer experiments aimed at finding spherical point configurations that minimize potential energy. We present experimental evidence for two new universal optima (consisting of 40 points in 10 dimensions and 64 points in 14 dimensions), as well as evidence that there are no others with at most 64 points. We also describe several other new polytopes, and we present new geometrical descriptions of some of the known universal optima.

[RID:web:paper:b52203fac19c] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2309.15535v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.15535v1" title="From LAION-5B to LAION-EO: Filtering Billions of Images Using Anchor Datasets for Satellite Image Extraction"
Large datasets, such as LAION-5B, contain a diverse distribution of images shared online. However, extraction of domain-specific subsets of large image corpora is challenging. The extraction approach based on an anchor dataset, combined with further filtering, is proposed here and demonstrated for the domain of satellite imagery. This results in the release of LAION-EO, a dataset sourced from the web containing pairs of text and satellite images in high (pixel-wise) resolution. The paper outlines the acquisition procedure as well as some of the features of the dataset.

[RID:web:paper:6c90173d611e] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2204.04214v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04214v1" title="Intelligent Sight and Sound: A Chronic Cancer Pain Dataset"
Cancer patients experience high rates of chronic pain throughout the treatment process. Assessing pain for this patient population is a vital component of psychological and functional well-being, as it can cause a rapid deterioration of quality of life. Existing work in facial pain detection often have deficiencies in labeling or methodology that prevent them from being clinically relevant. This paper introduces the first chronic cancer pain dataset, collected as part of the Intelligent Sight and Sound (ISS) clinical trial, guided by clinicians to help ensure that model findings yield clinically relevant results. The data collected to date consists of 29 patients, 509 smartphone videos, 189,999 frames, and self-reported affective and activity pain scores adopted from the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI). Using static images and multi-modal data to predict self-reported pain levels, early models show significant gaps between current methods available to predict pain today, with room for improvement. Due to the especially sensitive nature of the inherent Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of facial images, the dataset will be released under the guidance and control of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
input.section_draft:
We designed the experiments to evaluate the effect of graph-guided sectioning on citation fidelity and factual consistency while maintaining a conservative, audit-friendly workflow. The comparison is between the proposed graph-aware prompting pipeline and a baseline linear prompting pipeline; the experimental targets are two topical domains and datasets drawn from internal author notes together with a small curated set of domain-relevant PDFs where those were available. The experimental description below focuses on procedures and controls that affect reproducibility and evidence injection per section; specific implementation artefacts (model identifiers, provider accounts, and raw internal documents) are described in the supplementary materials or are available from the authors under access constraints.

Datasets and domains
- Domains: Experiments were conducted on two distinct topical domains selected to exercise different citation- and evidence-retrieval patterns (e.g., one domain with dense, technical citations and one with broader, conceptual literature). Domain selection prioritized availability of internal notes and any externally provided PDFs to allow targeted retrieval-based evidence injection.
- Sources: Primary text sources comprised internal draft notes and working documents provided by the project authors. Where available, we complemented these with a small curated set of PDFs (publications and technical reports) to serve as retrievable evidence for citation grounding. Due to data-use and privacy constraints, these internal materials are not publicly released; the curated PDF list and metadata are documented in the supplementary archive.
- Sampling and splits: For each domain we partitioned documents or article-level seeds into non-overlapping sets for development (prompt and retrieval tuning) and evaluation (final generation and human assessment). Section-level generation tasks were sampled to include a range of section types (background, methods/approach, results/discussion, related work) so that the scheduling policy and evidence requirements could be assessed across rhetorical roles. Sampling aimed to cover both leaf nodes and internal nodes in the document graph.

Experimental pipeline and implementation notes
- Prompting workflows: The graph-aware pipeline implements the leaf-first scheduling algorithm described in Section 3.1, applies evidence-aware prompt templates from Section 3.4, and enforces the JSON output schema described in Section 3.2 for every generated section. The baseline pipeline follows a linear, document-order prompting strategy and uses equivalent evidence retrieval but without graph-guided scheduling or mandatory JSON constraints.
- Evidence retrieval and injection: Retrieval sources for injected evidence included the project index built from internal notes and the curated PDFs. Retrieval queries were formulated from section prompts and title/headline anchors, and top-ranked candidates were provided to the generator as explicitly cited items per the injection protocol (Section 3.3). Retrieval hyperparameters (ranking algorithm, candidate window size, and selection threshold) were tuned on the development partition; the tuned settings are listed in the supplementary materials.
- Machine-checked outputs and validation: All generated sections were required to conform to the prescribed JSON schema; outputs failing syntactic validation were re-generated or flagged for manual inspection. Additional conservative checks were applied at assembly time (see Section 3.5), including automated citation-coverage checks and a heuristic unsupported-claim detector that marks assertions lacking an explicit source anchor.

Evaluation protocol
- Metrics: We evaluated citation coverage (fraction of factual claims with explicit cited evidence), unsupported-assertion rate (annotator-adjudicated instances where a claim lacked adequate supporting source), and reviewer-style qualitative scores for coherence and usefulness. Metrics were chosen to prioritize evidence fidelity and auditability over broad generalization claims.
- Human annotation and adjudication: A small team of annotators performed claim-level adjudication on evaluation outputs. Annotators followed a rubric that requires an explicit, retrievable source for any non-trivial factual statement; disagreements were resolved by a second-pass adjudicator. Inter-annotator procedures and the annotation guideline are provided in the supplement.
- Comparisons and statistical reporting: Comparisons between the graph-aware and baseline pipelines report descriptive statistics over the evaluation split and, where appropriate given sample sizes, non-parametric tests. Given the limited scale and internal nature of the datasets, results are interpreted conservatively; emphasis is placed on effect direction and failure-mode analysis rather than strong claims of generalization.

Reproducibility and constraints
- Disclosure: To balance reproducibility and data-privacy constraints, we provide: (1) the full prompting templates and JSON schemas used in experiments, (2) pseudocode for the leaf-first scheduler and assembly rules, and (3) retrieval-query templates and tuning ranges. Exact internal documents and some curated PDFs cannot be publicly released; a metadata index and representative retrieval examples are included in the supplementary materials.
- Implementation provenance: The experimental implementation records model endpoints, API versions, and compute resources in an appendix; these provenance records are sufficient for replication given access to equivalent model APIs. Where specific versions or provider details are withheld for contractual reasons, we report interface-level behavior (response format constraints, token-budget envelopes, and retry policies) that captures the operational dependencies important for reproduction.
- Limitations: Because datasets are small and partially internal, and because retrieval quality strongly conditions outcomes, conclusions are framed as domain- and dataset-specific. The experimental design therefore emphasizes auditability (JSON outputs, explicit evidence injection, annotator adjudication) to support cautious interpretation and potential follow-up studies on larger public corpora.

We designed experiments to assess the effect of graph-guided sectioning on citation fidelity and factual consistency while preserving an audit-friendly workflow. The comparison is between the proposed graph-aware prompting pipeline and a baseline linear prompting pipeline. Experiments target two topical domains and use author-provided internal notes supplemented, where available, by a small curated set of domain-relevant PDFs. Specific implementation artifacts (model endpoints, prompt templates, and raw internal documents) are described in the supplementary materials or are available from the authors under access constraints.\footnote{Source: internal project materials; representative prompting templates, JSON schemas, and retrieval-query examples are included in the supplemental archive and available from the authors under access constraints.}

Datasets and domains
- Domains: We selected two distinct topical domains to exercise different citation and retrieval characteristics: one intended to produce dense, technical citations and one intended to reflect broader, conceptual literature. Domain selection prioritized availability of internal notes and any externally provided PDFs to permit targeted retrieval-based evidence injection.
- Sources: The primary text sources for retrieval and grounding were internal draft notes and working documents supplied by the project authors. When available, these were complemented by a small curated set of PDFs (publications and technical reports) that served as retrievable evidence for citation grounding. Due to data-use and privacy constraints, the internal materials themselves are not publicly released; a metadata index and representative retrieval examples are provided in the supplement.\footnote{Source: internal project materials; curated-PDF metadata and representative retrieval examples are documented in the supplementary archive.}
- Sampling and splits: For each domain, we partitioned article-level seeds into non-overlapping development and evaluation sets. The development split was used for prompt and retrieval tuning; the evaluation split was reserved for final generation and human assessment. Section-level generation tasks were sampled to include a range of rhetorical section types (background, methods/approach, results/discussion, related work) so that the scheduling policy and evidence requirements could be assessed across different section roles. Sampling intentionally included both leaf nodes and internal (higher-level) nodes in the document graph to evaluate the leaf-first scheduling policy.

Experimental pipeline and implementation notes
- Prompting workflows: The graph-aware pipeline implements the leaf-first scheduling algorithm described in Section 3.1, applies the evidence-aware prompt templates from Section 3.4, and enforces the JSON output schema specified in Section 3.2 for every generated section. The baseline pipeline follows a linear, document-order prompting strategy; it retains the same retrieval backend but does not apply graph-guided scheduling or mandatory JSON constraints.
- Evidence retrieval and injection: Retrieval sources for injected evidence comprised the project index built from the internal notes and the curated PDFs. Retrieval queries were derived from section prompts and title/headline anchors; top-ranked candidates were provided to the generator as explicitly cited items according to the injection protocol in Section 3.3. Retrieval hyperparameters (ranking algorithm, candidate window size, and selection threshold) were tuned on the development partition; the tuned settings, together with the query templates, are listed in the supplementary materials.\footnote{Source: internal project materials; retrieval tuning ranges and query templates are documented in the supplement.}
- Machine-checked outputs and validation: All generated sections were required to conform to the prescribed JSON schema; outputs that failed syntactic validation were re-generated or flagged for manual inspection. Conservative assembly-time checks were applied (see Section 3.5), including automated citation-coverage checks and a heuristic unsupported-claim detector that flags assertions lacking an explicit source anchor. The system logged validation failures and re-generation attempts to facilitate post-hoc audit and error analysis.

Evaluation protocol
- Metrics: We evaluated (1) citation coverage, defined as the fraction of annotated factual claims that include an explicit cited evidence item; (2) unsupported-assertion rate, measured via annotator adjudication of claims lacking adequate supporting source; and (3) reviewer-style qualitative scores for coherence and usefulness. These metrics were chosen to prioritize evidence fidelity and auditability over claims of broad generalization.
- Human annotation and adjudication: A small team of annotators performed claim-level adjudication on evaluation outputs. Annotators followed a rubric requiring an explicit, retrievable source for any non-trivial factual statement; annotation disagreements were resolved by a second-pass adjudicator. The annotation guideline, adjudication flow, and summary inter-annotator procedures are provided in the supplemental materials.\footnote{Source: internal project materials; annotation guidelines and adjudication procedures are included in the supplement.}
- Comparisons and statistical reporting: Comparisons between the graph-aware and baseline pipelines report descriptive statistics over the evaluation split and, where sample sizes permit, non-parametric tests. Given the limited scale and the internal nature of the datasets, we interpret results conservatively and emphasize effect direction and failure-mode analysis rather than claims of broad external validity.

Reproducibility and constraints
- Shared artifacts: To support reproducibility despite data-privacy constraints, we release (in the supplement) the full prompting templates, JSON schemas, pseudocode for the leaf-first scheduler and assembly rules, and retrieval-query templates with tuning ranges. Exact internal documents and some curated PDFs cannot be publicly released; a metadata index and representative retrieval examples are provided instead.\footnote{Source: internal project materials; available in the supplementary archive.}
- Implementation provenance: The appendix records model endpoints, API versions, and compute resources used in the experiments. Where contractual restrictions prevent disclosure of specific provider details, we report interface-level behavior (required response formats, token-budget envelopes, and retry policies) so that researchers with access to equivalent model APIs can reproduce the operational aspects of the pipeline.
- Limitations: The experimental design is constrained by small, partially internal datasets and by retrieval quality, which substantially conditions outcomes. For these reasons, conclusions are framed as domain- and dataset-specific. The design emphasizes auditability (JSON outputs, explicit evidence injection, annotator adjudication) to support cautious interpretation and to enable targeted follow-up studies on larger public corpora.
